analysis.one_liner: Strengthens workers' rights to unionize, bargain collectively, and strike, with new penalties for employers who violate labor law.
analysis.headline: The House passed the bill 225-206 on March 9, 2021, but the Senate took no action, and it died at the end of the 117th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The PRO Act would make it easier for workers to form unions and harder for employers to block them. It broadens who counts as an employee covered by labor law, bans mandatory anti-union meetings, requires faster union elections with remote voting, lets unions collect fees from all workers in a unit even in states that ban it, allows sympathetic strikes at other companies, bans forced arbitration of workplace disputes, and raises fines for employers who illegally fire or retaliate against union supporters, up to $50,000 per violation and more for repeat offenders.
analysis.who_benefits: Private-sector workers, especially those trying to organize unions or already represented by one. The bill would extend coverage to many independent contractors and franchise and staffing-firm workers by treating companies that share control over workers as joint employers, speed up union elections so employers have less time to campaign against them, let workers vote by phone or internet, end the practice of permanently replacing strikers, and give workers who win back-pay cases full back pay, double damages, and the right to sue in court. It also voids agreements that require workers to give up their right to join class actions over employment disputes.

how_it_helps.text: Broadens the definitions of employee, supervisor, and employer so more workers are covered by federal labor protections, including many independent contractors and workers at franchised or subcontracted companies.

Makes it an unfair labor practice for an employer to require or coerce employees to attend anti-union meetings, and bans agreements that force employees to give up the right to pursue collective or class-action litigation over workplace disputes.
Speeds up union representation elections, requires remote voting by phone or internet, and takes away an employer's right to participate in or challenge election proceedings.
Prohibits permanently replacing or discriminating against striking workers, and protects intermittent and shorter strikes from being banned.

Raises penalties for employer violations to up to $50,000 per violation, doubled to $100,000 for repeat offenders, adds personal liability for directors and officers, and lets workers sue in court for back pay, consequential damages, and twice that amount as liquidated damages, without reductions based on interim earnings.

Overrides state right-to-work laws by allowing union contracts to require all workers in a bargaining unit to pay fees for representation, and permits unions to organize secondary strikes and boycotts.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who fight unionization, including gig-economy platforms, franchise chains, and staffing firms, which would face higher fines, faster elections, joint-employer liability, and greater exposure to lawsuits. Employers generally would face binding arbitration if first-contract negotiations stall after 120 days. Workers who prefer not to join a union but are in an organized unit would have to pay representation fees regardless of state right-to-work laws.

drawbacks.text: The bill lets union contracts require all workers in a bargaining unit to pay fees, overriding state right-to-work laws, which critics said forces workers to fund organizations they chose not to join.

The bill removes the legal prohibition on secondary strikes, allowing unions to pressure one employer by striking at another company that does business with it, and forbids employers from suing unions that do so.

If a newly organized workplace and its employer cannot reach a first contract within roughly four months, a three-member arbitration panel would impose a binding contract for two years, replacing negotiated agreement with an imposed one.
Banning forced arbitration agreements would also stop employers and workers from using a faster, cheaper individual dispute forum, pushing all employment disputes into class actions or court.
The ABC independent-contractor test could reclassify some workers who prefer the flexibility of contracting as employees, a concern raised by gig-work platforms and freelancers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers trying to organize, the bill addresses the main reasons union drives fail: long election delays, employer pressure meetings, retaliation with weak penalties, and permanent striker replacement. Those are significant, enforceable gains. The serious tradeoffs are on the other side: mandatory representation fees override the choices of roughly half the states, the imposed first-contract arbitration removes bargaining flexibility, and the broad joint-employer and contractor rules could catch businesses and workers who did nothing anti-union. On balance it is a major expansion of worker bargaining power with real costs concentrated on employers that oppose unions, though a few provisions also bind unwilling workers.

outcome.mechanism: The House passed it 225-206 on March 9, 2021, but the Senate never voted on it, and it died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

narrative.text: The House passed the bill on March 9, 2021, by a vote of 225 to 206, with 220 of 221 Democrats voting yes and 5 of 211 Republicans joining them.
A Republican motion to recommit, which would have sent the bill back to committee, failed 206 to 218 along party lines.
The Senate received the bill on March 11, 2021, and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions, where no further action was recorded.
The bill never received a Senate vote and expired at the end of the 117th Congress on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that oppose unionization, particularly companies that rely on misclassifying workers as independent contractors, pressuring employees against unions, or forcing disputes into arbitration, are better off because the bill never reached a Senate vote. Union-backed legislation of this scope has not advanced again in the same form.

for.name: Rep. Bobby Scott
for.role: Sponsor; Chair, House Education and Labor Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and managed it through House consideration, including two en bloc amendments.

for.name: 220 of 221 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted yes on passage; 210 had cosponsored the bill.

for.name: House Majority Leader Steny Hoyer
for.what_they_did: Scheduled the bill for floor consideration under a rule allowing one hour of debate.

for.name: President Joe Biden
for.what_they_did: Publicly called on Congress to pass the PRO Act as a priority of his administration.

against.name: 206 of 211 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on passage; voted 206-0 for the motion to recommit that would have returned the bill to committee.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for the bill in the Senate
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred on March 11, 2021.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote, with a 50-50 chamber and no clear path to 60 votes.

against.name: Rep. Jim Banks
against.what_they_did: Moved to recommit the bill to the House Committee on Education and Labor.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and major business groups
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, lobbying House members to oppose it and Senate offices to keep it off the floor.

sides.party_line_note: The House vote split almost entirely by party: 220 of 221 Democrats voted yes and 206 of 211 Republicans voted no, with 5 Republicans in favor and 1 Democrat opposed.

industries.note: The bill would sharply expand unions' organizing ability, bargaining leverage, and legal protections, and let them collect fees from all workers in organized units. Union growth historically raises pay for both members and nonmembers in organized markets.

The bill's independent-contractor test and joint-employer standard would reclassify many contract workers as employees with collective bargaining rights, undermining the staffing and gig business models that depend on classifying workers out of labor-law coverage.

The joint-employer definition would make brands and parent companies liable for labor practices at their franchisees and contractors, a structure many use to keep labor costs and liability at arm's length.

The bill would require disclosure of paid consultants who run anti-union campaigns, ban mandatory captive-audience meetings, and cut the window for challenging NLRB decisions from six months to 180 days, shrinking the market for counter-organizing services.

Employers would face fines up to $50,000 per violation, doubled to $100,000 for repeat offenders, worker lawsuits with double damages, faster elections, and binding arbitration of stalled first contracts. Some employers benefit from stable imposed contracts, but the net effect raises their labor costs and reduces their control over organizing outcomes.
